name: Oghenekevwe 'Kev' Dasilva-Strand
description: A deliberately retro filmmaker who shoots exclusively on flat-screen projection, Dasilva-Strand considers neural-feed cinema a 'colonization of the last private space' and has published several manifestos on the subject. His films — dense, slow, often four hours or longer — are distributed physically on data chips and have never been licensed to any broadcast network. Working out of a converted water-treatment facility in the Shelf, he has directed eleven features in thirty years, each one hand-assembled by a rotating crew of unpaid collaborators.
cultural_impact: He is credited with founding the Flat Doctrine movement, a loose philosophy among Shelf filmmakers that flat-screen is the only honest medium remaining.
story_hooks: A Tier 4 collector offers an obscene sum for the original data-chip masters of his entire catalog — and the offer is almost certainly a corporate acquisition attempt in disguise.
One of his unpaid collaborators leaks that his most celebrated film contains stolen neural-feed capture used without subjects' consent, complicating his anti-BCI ethics.
He is approached by a corponation defector who wants to fund his next film in exchange for dramatizing their testimony — and the material is genuinely explosive.
